task_row_model.query: Design a high-performance lock-free multiple-producer multiple-consumer (MPMC) queue in C++17 for x86-64. Provide a concrete algorithm and data layout, the precise std::atomic memory_order semantics for enqueue/dequeue, strategies to avoid the ABA problem, and a practical, lock-free node-reclamation approach that works under heavy contention without global locks.

documents.content: The Michael-Scott (MS) unbounded lock-free queue uses a linked-list of nodes with atomic head and tail pointers. Enqueue appends a new node by CAS-ing tail->next and then swinging tail; dequeue advances head and returns the next node. It is MPMC and widely used; correctness relies on careful CAS ordering. Implementations in C++ use std::atomic<Node*> and compare_exchange_weak/strong with acquire/release semantics around pointer updates. The MS queue requires a safe reclamation scheme because nodes are freed asynchronously; without reclamation it is simple, but production use needs hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation to avoid use-after-free.
documents.reasoning_trace: Identify MS queue as an MPMC linked-list algorithm; note it describes CAS-based enqueue/dequeue and mentions the need for reclamation. Explains atomic pointer usage and general memorder directions but lacks exact per-operation memory_order mapping, slot layout, and a concrete low-level avoidance of ABA for pointer reuse.

documents.content: A traditional producer-consumer pattern in C++ uses std::queue<T> guarded by std::mutex and std::condition_variable. Producers lock, push, notify_one; consumers wait on the condition variable and pop under lock. For high throughput tune malloc()/allocator, use move semantics and batch notifications. This approach is simple and robust and avoids complex ABA or reclamation concerns because memory lifetimes are serialized by the mutex. However, it is not lock-free and will suffer under very high thread counts and contention compared to atomic-based designs.
documents.reasoning_trace: Describes mutex-based queue and synchronization primitives. Relevant to concurrent queues broadly but irrelevant to the request for a lock-free MPMC design with atomic memory orders and lock-free reclamation; it does not provide atomic algorithms or lock-free reclamation techniques.

documents.content: A practical high-performance MPMC design is Dmitry Vyukov's bounded circular array with per-slot sequence counters. Layout: an array of slots each with T value and an atomic<uint64_t> seq padded to a cache line; head and tail are atomics of uint64_t indices. Enqueue reads tail, computes index=tail % N, checks slot.seq==tail, writes value, then uses atomic_compare_exchange to advance tail; producers use memory_order_relaxed for index ops, release on store to slot and acquire on subsequent reads. Sequence counters avoid ABA because each cycle changes seq. For unbounded needs, use an MS-style linked list plus hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation (per-thread retire lists and deferred free) to reclaim nodes without global locks.
documents.reasoning_trace: Presents Vyukov bounded MPMC algorithm and exact data layout (per-slot seq, padded cache-line), outlines index/tail logic and when to use relaxed/release/acquire semantics, and explains ABA avoidance via sequence counters. Also provides unbounded alternative and names lock-free reclamation strategies (hazard pointers, epoch) with how they integrate.

documents.content: Epoch-based reclamation (EBR) and hazard pointers are two lock-free memory reclamation techniques. EBR assigns a global epoch counter and each thread announces the epoch it is in; retired nodes are kept in per-thread lists tagged with the current epoch and only freed after no thread remains in older epochs. Hazard pointers let a thread publish pointers it may access so deleters scan hazard lists before freeing. Implementing hazard pointers in C++ requires atomic lists of hazards and periodic scans; EBR is cheaper but requires threads to periodically quiesce. Both avoid a single global lock and are compatible with MPMC queues when used to retire nodes safely.
documents.reasoning_trace: Explains two reclamation schemes in detail: mechanics of epochs and hazard pointers, per-thread retire lists, and scanning rules. Relevant to the reclamation part of the query but does not describe the queue algorithm or the precise memory_order usage inside enqueue/dequeue.

documents.content: False sharing and cache-line alignment drastically affect multithreaded throughput. Align frequently updated atomic counters and head/tail indices on separate cache lines (use alignas(64) or pad structs) to prevent ping-ponging between sockets. Structure data to keep producer-local and consumer-local fields separate, avoid pointer chasing across hot cache lines, and prefer contiguous arrays for spatial locality. These optimizations apply to many concurrent containers and reduce stalls, but they do not by themselves specify synchronization algorithms or memory_order semantics required for lock-free correctness.
documents.reasoning_trace: Covers cache-alignment and data-layout optimizations: padding, alignas, separating hot fields. Useful for performance tuning of concurrent queues but does not provide lock-free algorithmic details nor reclamation mechanisms, so it's tangential rather than an answer.
